slides.text: I worked the grueling night shift at the city hospital, running on stale coffee and pure adrenaline. Every morning at 5:00 AM, exhausted and numb, I’d walk past a small corner bakery. The grumpy, tattooed baker was always there, kneading dough in the window. We never spoke. But one freezing December morning, I found a warm chocolate croissant sitting on the bench outside, wrapped in a napkin. Scrawled on it were three words: 'For the bags under your eyes.'

It became our silent ritual. Every Tuesday and Thursday, a fresh pastry waited on the bench. Sometimes a brioche, sometimes a cinnamon roll. The napkins became my only tether to sanity. 'Tough night? Sugar helps,' or 'You save lives; I bake bread. Equal trades.' I started leaving tiny notes back: 'Patient stabilized. Croissant saved my life.' I fell hopelessly in love with a man I had never spoken to, memorizing the flour dusted on his muscular forearms.

On Valentine's Day, my shift ended early. I stood outside the bakery at 4:00 AM, my heart hammering. He was unlocking the door. When he saw me, he froze, a tray of tarts in his hands. Up close, his rough exterior completely betrayed the terrifyingly soft blush spreading across his cheeks. 'I'm early,' I whispered. He set the tray down, wiped his hands on his apron, and gave a nervous, breathtaking smile. 'I've been waiting for you to be early for six months.'
